summary: This is a cylindrical specimen of a low-density high-strength Fe-Mn-Al-C steel (Fe-25.14Mn-10Al-1.46C-0.053Nb) that was subjected to isothermal constant-strain-rate hot compression on a Gleeble-3500 thermo-mechanical simulator at 1000 °C and a strain rate of 0.01 s⁻¹ to a maximum 60% reduction (true strain 0.92), followed by water-spray quenching. The specimen is one condition of a systematic hot-deformation campaign (900–1150 °C, 0.01–10 s⁻¹) aimed at understanding the rheological behaviour, dynamic recrystallization (DRX) and microstructure evolution of the steel; its deformation condition lies within the 950–1000 °C / 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹ window identified as giving sufficient, relatively fine and uniform DRX.
composition: Nominal chemical composition (mass fraction, %): 1.46 C, 25.14 Mn, 10 Al, 0.053 Nb, balance Fe. The material is a low-density high-strength Fe-Mn-Al-C steel, chosen for its good corrosion resistance, low density and favourable combination of mechanical properties for automotive lightweighting, crash safety and complex service conditions. Mn and Al are the principal alloying additions alongside C, with a small Nb addition (0.053%).
processing: The specimen was cut from a forged billet into a cylinder of Φ8 mm × 12 mm with the two end faces kept perpendicular. Mica foils with high-temperature lubricant were affixed to both end faces to reduce friction and deformation non-uniformity. The Gleeble-3500 thermomechanical schedule was: heating to 1200 °C at 10 °C/s; homogenization by holding at 1200 °C for 120 s; cooling at 5 °C/s to the set test temperature of 1000 °C; isothermal holding at 1000 °C for 15 s so that the temperature inside and outside the sample equalized; isothermal constant-strain-rate compression at 1000 °C and 0.01 s⁻¹ to a maximum compression of 60% (corresponding to a maximum true strain of 0.92); finally water-spray cooling (quenching) to cool the steel down. This schedule is one point of the alloy's full test matrix (T = 900–1150 °C, ε̇ = 0.01–10 s⁻¹).
microstructure: The pre-deformation (as-forged) reference state consists of large polygonal grains outlined by bright, continuous, slightly etched boundaries and enclosing dark grey interiors; within essentially every grain there are many fine, closely spaced parallel light-grey striations/lamellae whose direction changes from grain to grain, giving a strongly banded dendritic/interdendritic segregation contrast rather than a uniform solid solution, indicating chemical heterogeneity in the as-forged condition. After 60% hot compression the specimen develops three deformation zones: 1 = difficult deformation zone, 2 = small deformation zone and 3 = large deformation zone, with the degree of dynamic recrystallization ranked zone 3 > zone 2 > zone 1. For this 1000 °C / 0.01 s⁻¹ condition, which lies within the 950–1000 °C / 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹ regime regarded as giving sufficient DRX, the recrystallized grain structure is relatively fine and uniform; more generally the recrystallized grains grow and microstructure heterogeneity improves as the strain rate decreases, and the DRX average grain size (measured from the core/large-deformation zone) increases with decreasing strain rate or increasing temperature.
properties: Mechanical/thermo-mechanical behaviour was characterized by isothermal constant-strain-rate hot compression on a Gleeble-3500 simulator (cylindrical Φ8 mm × 12 mm specimens, 60% / true strain 0.92, lubricated mica-foil end faces, water-spray quenched after compression). The steel behaves as a negative temperature-sensitive and positive strain-rate-sensitive material, i.e. flow stress rises with increasing strain rate and falls with increasing temperature; every flow curve shows an early peak followed by softening to a plateau. For this sample's condition (1000 °C, 0.01 s⁻¹) the Zener-Hollomon parameter is lnZ = 58.69 (Table 1). At the low strain rate of 0.01 s⁻¹ the alloy's peak stress decreases from 305.4 MPa at 900 °C to 53.8 MPa at 1150 °C, an 82% reduction (the 1000 °C value is not separately tabulated). Microstructure was examined by optical metallography using a LEXT OLS4000 laser confocal microscope on axially split, ground, polished and etched specimens (etchant: 30% nitric acid alcohol solution, volume fraction), with a 100 µm scale bar. No tensile, hardness, physical, chemical or radiation property data are reported for this sample.
mechanisms: Increasing temperature raises grain-boundary mobility, thermal activation, atomic diffusion and dislocation motion, strengthening the softening effect and lowering slip resistance, so the flow stress and peak stress decrease with increasing T (negative temperature sensitivity).

Decreasing strain rate gives dislocations more time to undergo dynamic recovery (DRV) and dynamic recrystallization (DRX), so the softening effect outweighs work hardening and the flow stress decreases; conversely higher strain rate shortens deformation time, reduces dislocation propagation, and leaves DRV/DRX insufficient, raising peak stress (positive strain-rate sensitivity).

A lower Zener-Hollomon parameter (Z = ε̇·exp(Qp/RT)), achieved by increasing T or decreasing strain rate, makes DRX initiation and completion easier, because both the critical strain εc and the steady-state strain εs of DRX increase with increasing Z.

Higher temperature promotes DRX because dislocation motion is a thermally activated process; the enhanced atomic oscillation/diffusion and grain-boundary migration effectively induce and complete DRX, but also accelerate recrystallized-grain growth, so a low T with high ε̇ tends to give fine yet incomplete DRX while a high T with low ε̇ gives complete but coarse grains.

During hot compression, friction between the specimen and the compression platens produces a non-uniform stress distribution, generating the three deformation zones (difficult, small and large deformation) in which the driving force for DRX, and hence the degree of recrystallization, is ranked zone 3 > zone 2 > zone 1.
conclusions: This specimen represents the 1000 °C / 0.01 s⁻¹ point of the alloy's hot-deformation matrix and falls inside the processing window (950–1000 °C / 0.01–0.1 s⁻¹, together with 1050–1100 °C / 1–10 s⁻¹) at which hot working produces sufficient dynamic recrystallization with a relatively fine and uniform grain structure. For the steel overall, the DRX activation energy was determined as 669.844 kJ mol⁻¹ from the Arrhenius hyperbolic-sine analysis; the critical/peak/steady-state stress and strain models were built against the Zener-Hollomon parameter (e.g. εc = 0.0093 lnZ − 0.43; εp = 0.020 lnZ − 0.94; εs = 0.034 lnZ − 1.53), and a DRX state diagram dividing work-hardening, partial-DRX and complete-DRX domains was drawn. Fine and uniform grains require avoiding both the under-recrystallized low-T/high-ε̇ regime and the coarsening high-T/low-ε̇ regime. A DRX average grain-size prediction model, d_rex = 807743.63 ε̇^(−0.1903) exp(−120648.47/RT) + 4.338, was established with R = 0.996 and MRE of only 4.53% and errors mostly below 3 µm, providing a reliable basis for predicting recrystallized grain size in hot-forged low-density high-strength steel.
unmapped: The dynamic recrystallization activation energy (669.844 kJ mol⁻¹), the Arrhenius hyperbolic-sine constants (α = 0.00599, k1 = 5.135, k2 = 15.690) and the lnZ map (Table 1) are material-level quantities derived from the whole test matrix (900–1150 °C, 0.01–10 s⁻¹), not unique to this single 1000 °C / 0.01 s⁻¹ condition; the fitted lines in Fig. 4a are not parallel, so Qp is only an average over the experimental range.

The paper also reports reproducibility checks (repeat experiments under identical conditions) and describes the Levenberg-Marquardt optimisation used to regress the grain-size model; these are method-level notes rather than properties of this specific sample.

Figure captions/labels contain a printing inconsistency (the 1150 °C, 1 s⁻¹ microstructure is labelled '(d)' instead of '(f)'), and several figure panels (Fig. 3a, 9, 10) are not specific to this sample alone but plot the full temperature/strain-rate matrix.
